1.open: Think of a time you had to wait through something hard, like a long recovery, a job search or a rough season. What helped you get through it?
questions: James says, "Consider it pure joy" when trials come (v. 2). What do you think he means, and what do you think he does not mean?
He says "the testing of your faith develops perseverance" (v. 3). Can you think of a hard time that left you steadier than before? What changed in you?

Verse 5 says God "gives generously to all without finding fault." What decision or situation in your life right now could use some wisdom, and how does it feel to hear that God does not scold us for asking?

James warns against doubting and calls the doubter "like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind" (v. 6). If you have ever struggled to trust God, how does this verse land with you? Be as honest as you like.
Verses 9 to 11 say the poor and the rich both have something to learn about where their worth comes from. Where do you find yourself tempted to measure your worth by what you have or lack?
James says that "each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away" (v. 14). Why might it be tempting to blame God or other people instead? What changes when we own our part?
Verse 19 says to be "quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger." Which of those three is hardest for you, and what usually sets it off?

James says to be "doers of the word, and not hearers only" (v. 22). Where is there a gap between what you hear in church or Scripture and what you actually do, and what is one small step toward closing it?
1.life: Pick one phrase from verses 19 to 22 and practice it this week. In one conversation where you would normally jump in, listen first. Then do one concrete thing you have been putting off that you already know is right.
1.prayer: Thank God that he gives generously and does not find fault when we ask. Ask for wisdom for one specific situation, and for strength to keep going for anyone in the group who is in a hard season.
1.tip: Verse 2 can sound like James is telling people to feel happy about suffering, which hurts someone who is grieving or struggling. Help the group hear it as hope that God can use hard times to build us, not as a demand to pretend we are fine. Verses 6 to 8 can also sting those who doubt, so make clear that honest questions are welcome in this room.

2.open: Think of a time you were new somewhere, like a church, a workplace or a school. What made you feel welcome, or not welcome?
questions: James describes a visitor in fine clothes getting a seat of honor while a poor visitor is told, "You must stand" (vv. 2-3). Why do you think we so easily treat people differently based on how they look or what they have?

James asks, "Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith" (v. 5). What do you think it means that God values people the way he does, and how does that challenge the way we measure people?
Verse 8 calls "Love your neighbor as yourself" the royal law. Who is a neighbor you find hard to love well right now, and what would it look like to treat them with real respect?
Verse 13 says, "Mercy triumphs over judgment." Where have you received mercy when you did not deserve it, and how did it change you?

James asks, "What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds?" (v. 14). What is the difference between saying we care and actually showing it? Where do you see that gap in your own life?
In verse 19 James says, "Even the demons believe that, and shudder." What do you think he means by saying belief alone is not enough?

Verse 24 says a person is justified "by his deeds and not by faith alone." Christians read this alongside Paul's teaching in different ways. What questions or doubts does this verse raise for you, and how do you make sense of it?
James ends with "faith without deeds is dead" (v. 26). If someone watched your week, what would they guess you believe? Where would you like that picture to be truer?
2.life: Pick one person this week who is easy to overlook, such as a newcomer, a neighbor in need or a coworker nobody talks to. Do one concrete thing for them, like sharing a meal, giving your time or simply sitting with them.
2.prayer: Ask God to show you where you play favorites without noticing. Pray that your faith would show up in practical love for the people he puts in front of you.
2.tip: Verse 24 can start a debate about Paul and James that eats the whole evening. Say plainly that Christians understand it differently: many read James as saying deeds show faith is real, while Catholic and Orthodox Christians tend to say faith and deeds together share in being made right with God, both as gifts of grace. Then bring the group back to the chapter's main point, that real faith shows up in how we treat people, and let anyone who wants to keep talking do so afterwards.

3.open: Think of a time a few words, kind or unkind, stuck with you for years. What was it?
questions: James warns that "we who teach will be judged more strictly" (v. 1). Why do you think people who shape others with words carry extra weight? Who has shaped you that way?
James says, "We all stumble in many ways" (v. 2), and he includes himself. How does it change the way you read the chapter that he is not standing above his readers?
James compares the tongue to a bit in a horse's mouth, a small rudder and a spark (vv. 3-5). Which picture fits best for you, and why?
Verse 8 says "no man can tame the tongue." What do you make of that, and where do you find help with something you cannot fix by willpower alone?

In verse 9 we bless God and "curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness." How does remembering that every person is made in God's likeness change the way we talk about people who annoy or hurt us?
James asks whether "fresh water and salt water" can flow from the same spring (v. 11). When have your words sounded very different depending on who was listening, and what do you think that shows?

James says wisdom shows itself "by his good conduct" and "deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom" (v. 13), and he warns about "bitter jealousy and selfish ambition" (v. 14). Where do you see those two at work in everyday life, in yourself or around you?

Verse 17 describes wisdom from above as "pure, then peace-loving, gentle." Which word on that list feels furthest from you right now, and what would it look like to grow in it? If this chapter mostly leaves you feeling discouraged, you can say so honestly.
3.life: Pick one conversation, text or post this week where you would normally say something sharp or careless. Pause first, and ask God to help you say something true and kind instead. If you slip, tell God and try again.
3.prayer: Thank God that he is patient with us when our words go wrong. Ask him to guard your mouths and to give the group the kind of wisdom that is gentle and makes peace.
3.tip: The language about the tongue being "set on fire by hell" (v. 6) can sound harsh, and some people may feel crushed, especially if words have hurt them or if they have said things they regret. Keep the tone grace-first: James includes himself in "We all stumble," so let the group admit weakness without shame, and point to the hope in the wisdom from above.

4.open: What is something you made plans for that didn't turn out the way you expected?
questions: James asks, "What causes conflicts and quarrels among you?" and answers, "the passions at war within you" (v. 1). Think of a recent argument you were part of. How much of it came from something you wanted?
James says, "You do not have, because you do not ask" (v. 2). What do you find easy to worry about or chase on your own, but hard to bring to God?
Verse 3 says some prayers go unanswered because people ask "with wrong motives." How do you tell the difference between a good desire and a selfish one in your own prayers?

James calls friendship with the world "hostility toward God" (v. 4). Christians differ on how far to take that, some pointing to staying apart from the culture and others to greed, envy and status-seeking. Where do you see the pull of those things in daily life?
Verse 6 says, "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." What does humility look like in an ordinary day, and what makes it hard?

James tells his readers to "Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you" (v. 8), even while naming them "double-minded." If you feel pulled two ways about God right now, what would drawing near look like for you, even in a small step?
James says, "who are you to judge your neighbor?" (v. 12). Why is it so easy to talk down about other people, and what changes when we remember God is the one Judge?
James calls life "a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes" (v. 14). How does that land with you: as a worry, a relief, or something else? How might it change how you make plans?
4.life: Before your next plan, decision or disagreement this week, stop for a moment and ask God what you are really wanting. Then ask him for it, or hand it over.
4.prayer: Thank God that he "gives grace to the humble" and keeps giving more. Ask for a humble heart, honest words about other people, and trust with your plans.
4.tip: Verses 8 to 10 can sound harsh, as if God wants people miserable. Point the group to verse 6 and to the promise in verse 10, and read the call to mourn as an honest turning back, not a demand to feel awful. Also, verse 5 is unclear and Bible readers differ on what it means, so a short, plain mention is enough before moving on.

5.open: What is something you have had to wait a long time for, and how did you pass the time?
questions: James says the wages withheld from the workers "are crying out against you" (v. 4). What does this tell us about how God sees unfair pay and the people who suffer from it?
Verse 5 says the rich have lived "in luxury and self-indulgence." In our own day, where do you see money or comfort making people deaf to the needs of others? Where might that touch our own lives?
James says, "See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil" (v. 7). What does the farmer's kind of waiting look like, and how is it different from simply doing nothing?
In verse 9 James says, "Do not complain about one another." Why might waiting and hardship make us sharper with the people closest to us?
James holds up Job and says, "The Lord is full of compassion and mercy" (v. 11). Have you ever found that hard to believe in the middle of a difficult season? What was that like?
In verse 12 James tells us to let our yes mean yes and our no mean no, without swearing oaths. Where is it hardest for you to be plainly honest, and what makes it hard?
Verse 16 says, "Confess your sins to each other and pray for each other." What would make a group like ours a safe place to do that, and what might get in the way?
James writes that "Elijah was a man just like us" (v. 17). If you have ever prayed and not seen the answer you hoped for, what has that done to your prayers? Say as much or as little as you like.
5.life: Pick one person you could pray with this week, in person or by phone, and ask how you can pray for them. Then keep it simple and actually pray together.
5.prayer: Ask God for patience in whatever you are waiting on right now. Pray for anyone in the group who is sick, worn down, or has drifted from faith.
5.tip: Verses 14 and 15 can be painful for anyone who prayed for healing and did not receive it. Say gently that Christians understand these verses differently, including the oil and how sure the promise of healing is, and that no one in the room is being blamed for how their prayers turned out. Keep the focus on caring for each other.
